docs.title: Snippy-NG
docs.text:
Snippy-NG is the next generation of microbial variant calling with Snippy. It provides command-line pipelines for assembly, short-read, long-read, and multi-sample SNP analysis, plus tools for core alignment construction, phylogenetic tree building, and interactive report generation.

Snippy-NG is under active development and should not replace Snippy for production analyses without validation.

Follow progress on the Snippy-NG Development Blog.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
For most users, install the complete Snippy-NG environment with:

curl -sSL https://cpg.org.au/snippy-ng/install.sh | bash -s -- --force

The Python package is also available from PyPI:

pip install snippy-nextgen

The installed command is:

snippy-ng --help

See the installation guide for dependency details, Clair3 setup, and development installs.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: Command Purpose snippy-ng asm Assembly-based SNP calling from a reference and assembly FASTA. snippy-ng short Short-read SNP calling from paired-end reads or an existing BAM. snippy-ng long Long-read SNP calling from FASTQ reads or an existing BAM. snippy-ng multi Run multi-sample analysis and construct a core alignment. snippy-ng core Create a core alignment from multiple Snippy-NG run directories. snippy-ng tree Build a phylogenetic tree from an alignment. snippy-ng gui Launch the optional Gradio graphical interface. Utilities See utilities for details. Also includes ref, gather, samclip, cnv, and report commands.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Run assembly-based SNP calling:

snippy-ng asm --ref tests/data/reference.gbk --asm tests/data/wildtype.contigs.fa

Run short-read SNP calling:

snippy-ng short \
  --ref tests/data/reference.gbk \
  --R1 tests/data/mutant_R1.fastq.gz \
  --R2 tests/data/mutant_R2.fastq.gz

Run long-read SNP calling:

export CLAIR3_MODELS=./clair3_models
snippy-ng long --ref tests/data/JKD6159.fasta --reads tests/data/JKD6159.fastq.gz

Run a multi-sample workflow and build a report:

snippy-ng utils gather --json --ref tests/data/reference.gbk tests/data/{wildtype,mutant}* > samples.json
snippy-ng multi samples.json --cpus 6 -o multi
snippy-ng tree --fast multi/core/core.095.aln -o multi/tree
snippy-ng utils report tree multi/tree/tree.snps.newick --metadata multi/snippy.qc.tsv -o multi/report

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
To set up a development environment, clone the repository and install pixi and hatch.

git clone git@github.com:centre-pathogen-genomics/snippy-ng.git
cd snippy-ng
curl -fsSL https://pixi.sh/install.sh | bash
pixi global install hatch

Activate the pixi environment and launch a hatch shell:

pixi shell
hatch shell

Run the default fast test suite:

pixi run test

Run simulation-backed integration tests:

pixi run -e integration test-integration

docs.title: snippy-ng core
docs.text:
Turn finished Snippy-NG runs into a core alignment: one concatenated alignment of every sample against a shared reference, filtered down to the sites that are present in enough samples to be worth analysing, plus pairwise SNP distances.

Use it when the per-sample work is already done — for example on the samples/ directory of a snippy-ng multi run — and you want to choose the core threshold yourself, or re-run the alignment with different settings.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
snippy-ng core multi-phix/samples/* --ref multi-phix/reference/GCF_000819615.1.fa -o core-phix

Each SNIPPY_DIRS argument is a Snippy-NG run directory containing the sample's pseudo-genome (*.fna) and its QC table (*.qc.tsv). --ref is the reference FASTA — or a prepared reference directory, as produced by snippy-ng utils ref or by a previous run — used to define contig order. Unlike multi, core takes a local reference path, not an accession.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
Reusing the phiX174 run from Multi-sample analysis:

snippy-ng core multi-phix/samples/* --ref multi-phix/reference/GCF_000819615.1.fa -o core-phix

That finishes in a few seconds and produces an 8-sequence alignment (reference + 7 samples) of 43088 sites, which the soft-core filter reduces to 576 sites:

Output Result for this example core.full.aln 8 sequences, 43088 sites (every position in the reference) core.095.aln 8 sequences, 576 variable sites present in ≥95% of samples core.095.fconst 1273,1139,1233,1662 constant sites, for IQ-TREE -fconst core.095.distance.tsv pairwise SNP distances, e.g. phiX174-SCSC2 vs reference = 25

Continue straight to a tree:

snippy-ng tree --fast core-phix/core.095.aln -o core-phix/tree

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    S["Snippy-NG run directories (*.fna + *.qc.tsv)"] --> R[Load or prepare the reference]
    R --> C["Combine pseudo-genomes into core.full.aln (reference first)"]
    C --> D1["Pairwise SNP distances: core.full.distance.tsv"]
    C --> A["Per-sample aligned percentage: core.aligned.tsv"]
    A --> F{Alignment outlier check}
    F -->|flag off, default| K["core.filtered.aln: every sample kept"]
    F -->|--remove-alignment-outliers| X["core.filtered.aln: outliers dropped"]
    K --> SF["coresnpfilter -e -c CORE: core.095.aln + core.095.fconst"]
    X --> SF
    SF --> D2["Pairwise SNP distances: core.095.distance.tsv"]

The reference is written as the first sequence of the alignment, each sample contributes one concatenated supercontig per reference contig, and --mask (a BED file in reference coordinates) turns the masked regions into N in every sequence, including the reference.

docs.title: Strict core vs soft core
docs.text:
A site is core if an unambiguous base (A, C, G or T) is present there in at least the fraction of sequences given by --core. Gaps, N and any other character are treated the same way: as missing data. The comparison is ≥, so with --core 0.8 a site with 4 of 5 unambiguous bases still counts as core. Invariant sites are always removed, so the core alignment contains only variable sites.

--core 1.0 gives a strict core: only sites with data in every sample. The default --core 0.95 gives a soft core, which tolerates a little missing data at each site and therefore keeps many more sites as datasets grow. The trade-off is documented in Taouk et al., Exploring SNP filtering strategies: the influence of strict vs soft core (Microbial Genomics 2025;11(1):001346, doi:10.1099/mgen.0.001346):

  • A strict core shrinks markedly as sample size and genome diversity increase, discarding potentially informative data; in a 10 000-genome Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi alignment a 95% soft core yielded ten times more informative sites than a 100% strict core, with similar patterns in Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
  • Trees built from soft-core alignments generally showed better clock-like behaviour: the N. gonorrhoeae 95% soft-core phylogeny had a root-to-tip regression R² of 0.50 versus 0.21 for the strict-core phylogeny.
  • The paper's conclusion is that soft-core strategies are preferable for large, diverse datasets — which is why --core 0.95 is the default here.

The filtering is done by Core-SNP-filter (coresnpfilter --core CORE --exclude_invariant), the tool released with that paper. Its README has an illustrated example that colours the sites removed at different thresholds; the key points are that non-A/C/G/T characters are all treated as missing, that the core fraction test is inclusive, and that a site can be both invariant and non-core — invariant sites are filtered first.

The counts in core.095.fconst (invariant A,C,G,T counts) exist so that a tree built from a variable-sites-only alignment can correct for the sites that were removed, for example iqtree -fconst 1273,1139,1233,1662.

docs.title: Alignment outliers
docs.text:
The core alignment is only meaningful if the samples in it are comparable, so before filtering, core looks at the aligned percentage of each sample in core.full.aln: the fraction of its sites that are A/C/G/T rather than gaps or ambiguity codes. A sample with a low value (a poorly assembled genome, a contaminant, or a very divergent genome) adds gaps to every site it touches and can pull the whole alignment down.

Samples are grouped by fitting a one- to three-component Gaussian mixture to those percentages. Components are ordered by their means, the largest gap between adjacent means is the split, and everything above the split is "retained". The lower-alignment component(s) are the candidates for removal.

Each sample's probability_retained — its posterior probability of belonging to the retained component(s) — is compared with --alignment-outlier-threshold (default 0.20). Samples below the threshold are dropped. Because clusters are usually well separated, posteriors are near 0.0 or 1.0 and the exact threshold rarely changes the outcome; it matters for samples that fall between clusters.

Removal is off by default. With the flag off, nothing is removed and the run warns instead, naming the samples in the lower cluster:

Alignment core.full.aln splits into 2 clusters (largest gap 80.0 percentage points);
kept the lower-alignment cluster(s): s11, s12. Rerun with --remove-alignment-outliers
(threshold 0.20) to drop them, or inspect core.alignment-filter.tsv

To drop them:

snippy-ng core multi-phix/samples/* --ref reference.fa --remove-alignment-outliers -o core-phix

Small cohorts (fewer than 10 samples) are too small to fit a mixture model, so a robust one-sided MAD rule is used instead: samples far below the median aligned percentage are outliers, and --alignment-outlier-threshold is not used. The same warning/flag behaviour applies.

Every per-sample decision is recorded in core.alignment-filter.tsv (aligned, assigned_component, probability_retained, removed, filter_reason), and the run also checks whether the mixture components simply track the input type (pipeline_type from each sample's *.qc.tsv) in core.alignment-cluster-technical-check.tsv — a strong association means the clusters are technical, not biological.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Default Purpose SNIPPY_DIRS... – One or more Snippy-NG run directories (*.fna plus *.qc.tsv) --reference, --ref required Reference FASTA or prepared reference directory, used for contig order --core 0.95 Fraction of samples that must have an unambiguous base at a site for it to stay in the core alignment --remove-alignment-outliers disabled Drop detected low-alignment outlier samples before core filtering --alignment-outlier-threshold 0.20 Posterior probability of belonging to the retained clusters; only used with --remove-alignment-outliers and cohorts large enough for mixture modelling --snp-distance-format tabular Format of the pairwise SNP distance matrix: tabular or phylip --mask none BED file (reference coordinates) of regions to mask with N in every sequence

Global options (-o/--outdir, -p/--prefix, -c/--cpus, -r/--ram, --force, --skip-check, --create-missing, --no-cleanup, --quiet, --debug, ...) are shared with the other commands. Run snippy-ng core -h for the full list.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
With -o core-phix and the default -p core:

core-phix/
├── core.full.aln                          all samples, every reference position
├── core.full.distance.tsv                 pairwise SNP distances (full alignment)
├── core.aligned.tsv                       per-sample aligned percentage
├── core.filtered.aln                      alignment after the outlier check
├── core.alignment-filter.tsv              per-sample outlier decisions and mixture diagnostics
├── core.alignment-cluster-technical-check.tsv  do components track pipeline_type?
├── core.095.aln                           soft core alignment (suffix follows --core)
├── core.095.fconst                        invariant site counts for IQ-TREE -fconst
└── core.095.distance.tsv                  pairwise SNP distances (core alignment)

--core 1.0 writes core.100.aln; the same rule applies to the .fconst and .distance.tsv files. Every pipeline directory also gets LOG.txt, FILES.tsv, CITATIONS.txt and PIPELINE.txt.

docs.title: snippy-ng gui
docs.text:
Launch the optional Gradio graphical interface for running snippy-ng multi from a browser.

The GUI accepts a reference genome and sample files, creates a multi-sample configuration, runs the multi-sample pipeline, and provides output files for download.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
The GUI depends on Gradio, which is optional. Install Snippy-NG with the GUI extra:

pip install 'snippy-nextgen[gui]'

Or add Gradio to an existing Snippy-NG environment:

pip install gradio

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
Run the GUI locally:

snippy-ng gui

By default this starts a server on 127.0.0.1:7860 and opens the interface in your browser.

Use a different host or port:

snippy-ng gui --host 0.0.0.0 --port 7861

Do not open a browser automatically:

snippy-ng gui --no-browser

docs.title: Public Hosting
docs.text:
If you are hosting the GUI for other users, you should usually run it with both --temp-output and --no-server-paths:

snippy-ng gui --host 0.0.0.0 --temp-output --no-server-paths

--temp-output writes each GUI run under the Gradio/system temporary directory instead of the current working directory. This avoids filling the launch directory with user run outputs.

--no-server-paths hides the server-side path inputs and allows uploads only. This prevents users from entering arbitrary paths on the host running the GUI.

You can also ask Gradio to create a public share link:

snippy-ng gui --share --temp-output --no-server-paths

Only use --share when you are comfortable exposing the running GUI through Gradio's sharing service.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
By default the GUI supports two input modes:

  • Upload files from your computer.
  • Enter paths that already exist on the server.

Use --no-server-paths to disable server path entry:

snippy-ng gui --no-server-paths

This is the safer mode for public or shared deployments.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
After a run completes, the GUI shows the output directory and a file browser for downloading individual output files.

The GUI also includes a button to create a .tar.gz archive of the output directory on demand. The archive is created in a temporary directory when the button is clicked, not during the pipeline run.

By default, run output directories are created under the current working directory. Use --temp-output to place them under the Gradio/system temporary directory instead:

snippy-ng gui --temp-output

docs.title: Resource Limits
docs.text:
Use --max-cpus to cap the highest CPU value available in the GUI:

snippy-ng gui --max-cpus 16

This is useful on shared machines where you do not want GUI users to request all available cores.

docs.title: Command Options
docs.text: Option Default Purpose --host 127.0.0.1 Host interface for the GUI server. --port 7860 Port for the GUI server. --share disabled Create a public Gradio share link. --no-browser disabled Do not open the GUI in a browser. --temp-output disabled Write GUI run outputs under the Gradio/system temp directory. --max-cpus detected CPUs Maximum CPU value allowed in the GUI. --no-server-paths disabled Hide server-side path inputs and allow uploads only.

docs.title: snippy-ng multi
docs.text: Run SNP calling for many samples against one reference and build a core alignment from the results. Each sample can be short reads, long reads, or an assembly, so a single run can mix input types.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
snippy-ng utils gather --json --ref reference.gbk tests/data/*.fastq.gz > samples.json
snippy-ng multi samples.json --cpus 6 -o multi
snippy-ng tree --fast multi/core/core.095.aln -o multi/tree
snippy-ng utils report tree multi/tree/tree.snps.newick --metadata multi/snippy.qc.tsv -o multi/report

CONFIG may be a local path, - for stdin, or an HTTP(S) URL:

snippy-ng multi https://example.com/samples.json --ref reference.fasta
snippy-ng utils gather --ref reference.fasta --json | snippy-ng multi -

The reference is required, either from the config (JSON only) or from --ref. It may be a FASTA/GenBank file, a prepared reference directory, or an NCBI (GCF_/GCA_) or AllTheBacteria (SAMN/SAMEA) assembly accession, which is downloaded. The reference is prepared once into <outdir>/reference and reused by every sample.

docs.title: Worked example: phiX174
docs.text:
A complete run over a 5.4 kb phage genome that takes about 30 seconds and needs no data of your own. The config (docs/examples/phiX174-samples.json) lists six assemblies and one Illumina read set of phiX174, and the reference is given as an NCBI accession on the command line, so everything is downloaded for you:

snippy-ng multi docs/examples/phiX174-samples.json --ref GCF_000819615.1 -o multi-phix --cpus 4

The same config can be fetched over HTTP instead of read from disk:

snippy-ng multi \
    https://raw.githubusercontent.com/centre-pathogen-genomics/snippy-ng/main/docs/examples/phiX174-samples.json \
    --ref GCF_000819615.1 -o multi-phix --cpus 4

The run downloads the reference (GCF_000819615.1, 5386 bp) plus six phiX174 assemblies and one 1.8 MB Illumina run (ERR098007), calls variants for every sample, and builds the core alignment:

Output Result for this example snippy.qc.tsv 7 samples: 17–30 SNPs per assembly, 7 SNPs for ERR098007 (mean depth 48x) core/core.095.aln 8 sequences (reference + 7 samples), 576 variable sites snippy.failed.tsv header only, every sample succeeded

Continue with a tree and an interactive report:

snippy-ng tree --fast multi-phix/core/core.095.aln -o multi-phix/tree
snippy-ng utils report tree multi-phix/tree/tree.snps.newick --metadata multi-phix/snippy.qc.tsv -o multi-phix/report

This example needs network access to NCBI Datasets (reference and assemblies) and to SRA (the read set). Drop the phiX174-reads-ERR098007 sample if you only want the assembly path, which uses the NCBI Datasets API alone.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    C["CONFIG: JSON / CSV / TSV / URL / stdin"] --> R[Prepare reference once]
    R --> D[Pre-download read and assembly accessions]
    D --> S[Run one pipeline per sample, in parallel]
    S --> Q[Combine per-sample QC and breakdown tables]
    S --> F["Failed samples -> PREFIX.failed.tsv"]
    Q --> A[Core alignment + alignment outlier filtering]
    A --> O["core.095.aln, distance matrices, core QC"]

Accessions are resolved centrally into <outdir>/downloads before the parallel workers start, so a repeated accession is downloaded only once.

docs.title: JSON
docs.text:
{
  "reference": "SAMN16246485",
  "samples": {
    "mutant": {
      "type": "short",
      "left": "reads/mutant_R1.fastq.gz",
      "right": "reads/mutant_R2.fastq.gz"
    },
    "wildtype": {
      "type": "asm",
      "assembly": "assemblies/wildtype.fasta"
    },
    "outbreak-1": {
      "type": "long",
      "reads_accession": "SRR1234567"
    }
  }
}

reference is optional when --ref is given.

docs.title: CSV / TSV
docs.text:
The first row is a header. sample and type are required; every other column is a per-sample option, and empty cells are ignored. Because CSV/TSV cannot express nested values, use left/right for short reads. The reference must be given with --ref.

sample,type,left,right
mutant,short,reads/mutant_R1.fastq.gz,reads/mutant_R2.fastq.gz
wildtype,asm,assemblies/wildtype.fasta,

Sample names must be unique.

docs.title: Sample options
docs.text:
Key Applies to Purpose type all short, long, or asm (required) left, right short Read files; left alone means single-end reads short, long Read file(s); a string or a list of paths assembly asm Assembly FASTA reads_accession short, long SRA accession (SRR/ERR/DRR) to download assembly_accession asm NCBI (GCF_/GCA_) or AllTheBacteria (SAMN/SAMEA) accession bam short, long Use a pre-aligned BAM/CRAM instead of aligning reads vcf all Use an existing VCF instead of calling variants

Any other option accepted by the corresponding single-sample pipeline can also be set per sample, for example caller, model, aligner, min_depth, mask, or downsample. Keys that the pipeline does not accept are dropped with a debug log message. Samples are routed to the pipeline matching their type, and each one is written to its own directory, so samples never overwrite each other.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Default Purpose CONFIG – CSV, TSV, or JSON config, - for stdin, or an HTTP(S) URL --reference, --ref from JSON config Reference genome, prepared reference directory, or assembly accession --core 0.95 Fraction of samples a site must be present in to be kept in the core alignment --remove-alignment-outliers disabled Remove detected low-alignment outlier samples from the alignment before core filtering --alignment-outlier-threshold 0.20 Posterior probability threshold for retaining a sample in the alignment-percentage clusters; only used with --remove-alignment-outliers and cohorts large enough for mixture modelling --cpus-per-sample auto CPUs allocated to each sample pipeline --stop-on-failure disabled Stop the run as soon as any sample fails, instead of continuing

Global options (-o/--outdir, -p/--prefix, -c/--cpus, -r/--ram, --force, --skip-check, --create-missing, --no-cleanup, --quiet, --debug, ...) are shared with the other commands. Run snippy-ng multi -h for the full list.

docs.title: Parallelism
docs.text: Samples run in parallel, each in its own worker process. --cpus is the total CPU budget for the run: with --cpus-per-sample N each worker gets N CPUs and the number of workers is --cpus / N. Without --cpus-per-sample, the budget is split so that workers divide --cpus evenly, preferring fewer workers that each get a larger share (roughly one worker per four CPUs, capped at the number of samples).

docs.title: Alignment clusters
docs.text:
Before the core alignment is built, the per-sample aligned percentages are checked for low-alignment outliers. Nothing is removed by default: when the samples look like they split into clusters, or when a sample looks like a low-alignment outlier, snippy-ng prints a warning naming the affected samples and records the decision for every sample in core/core.alignment-filter.tsv.

Re-run with --remove-alignment-outliers to drop those samples:

snippy-ng multi samples.json --remove-alignment-outliers

For cohorts of ten or more samples the mixture model is used and --alignment-outlier-threshold sets how strict it is: a sample is removed when its posterior probability of belonging to the retained (higher-alignment) clusters falls below the threshold. Smaller cohorts use a robust one-sided MAD rule instead, where the flag alone enables removal and the threshold value is not used. See Core alignment for figures explaining the mixture model and the threshold.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
With -o multi and the default -p snippy:

multi/
├── reference/                     prepared reference (FASTA, .fai, .dict, .gff, metadata.json)
├── samples/<sample>/              one Snippy-NG run directory per successful sample
│   ├── snippy.all.vcf.gz
│   ├── snippy.pass.vcf
│   ├── snippy.tab
│   ├── snippy.fna
│   ├── snippy.qc.tsv
│   └── snippy.report.html
├── core/
│   ├── core.full.aln              all samples, ungapped alignment
│   ├── core.full.distance.tsv     pairwise SNP distance matrix (full alignment)
│   ├── core.aligned.tsv           per-sample aligned percentage
│   ├── core.filtered.aln          alignment after outlier filtering
│   ├── core.alignment-filter.tsv  per-sample filter decision
│   ├── core.alignment-cluster-technical-check.tsv
│   ├── core.095.aln               soft core alignment (suffix follows --core)
│   ├── core.095.fconst            constant-site counts for phylogenetic correction
│   └── core.095.distance.tsv      pairwise SNP distance matrix (core alignment)
├── snippy.qc.tsv                  combined per-sample QC, plus core_aligned_percent
├── snippy.vcf.breakdown.tsv       combined per-sample variant breakdown
└── snippy.failed.tsv              samples that failed, with the error message

-p/--prefix controls the sample outputs and the combined qc, vcf.breakdown and failed tables. Core alignment files always use the core prefix, and the --core value appears in the core alignment file names (0.95 → core.095.aln, 1.0 → core.100.aln). Files from accessions that were downloaded are cached under <outdir>/downloads.

docs.title: Failures
docs.text:
By default a failing sample does not stop the run: its error is recorded in <prefix>.failed.tsv, the sample is dropped, and the core alignment is built from the samples that succeeded. If every sample fails, the run stops with an error instead of producing an empty alignment.

With --stop-on-failure the run stops at the first failure and reports all samples that failed, which is useful in automated pipelines where a partial result is worse than no result.

docs.text:

  • Utilities: reference preparation, tree and sample reports

docs.title: One VCF file to rule them all
docs.text:
The snippy.all.vcf.gz produced by the asm, short, and long pipelines carries everything needed to rebuild the masked consensus FASTA (snippy.fna) with a few bcftools/bedtools commands. Beyond the real variant calls, the all-VCF encodes depth regions as synthetic records:

Kind Meaning Encoding Rebuilt as ZERODEPTH No aligned reads in the region Left-anchored symbolic deletion block: POS=<base before the region>, REF=<that base>, ALT="<DEL>", FILTER=ZERODEPTH, ID=DEL_n, INFO=TYPE=INDEL;ZERODEPTH;SVTYPE=DEL;END=...;SVLEN=-... - LOWDEPTH span Region below the min depth threshold (fixed --min-depth or auto median − 2·MAD) The same symbolic deletion block, marked with FILTER=LOWDEPTHSPAN, ID=LOWDEPTH_n, INFO=TYPE=LOWDEPTH;LOWDEPTH;SVTYPE=DEL;END=...;SVLEN=-... N

Example records:

Wildtype    35187   DEL_2   C   <DEL>   .   ZERODEPTH   TYPE=INDEL;ZERODEPTH;SVTYPE=DEL;END=35747;SVLEN=-560    GT  1/1
Wildtype    20  LOWDEPTH_1  G   <DEL>   .   LOWDEPTHSPAN    TYPE=LOWDEPTH;LOWDEPTH;SVTYPE=DEL;END=35187;SVLEN=-35167    GT  1/1

Both kinds are <DEL> blocks that the consensus step applies as deletions, so the depth regions come out as -; step 3 then masks the low-depth intervals with N, which is what the pipeline's own depth mask does. Because the block is symbolic, REF holds a single anchor base instead of the whole region — for the two records above that is the difference between ~35 kb of REF/ALT text and a handful of bytes.

A symbolic block needs a base before the region to anchor on, so two cases still use an explicit REF sequence:

  • a region that starts at position 1 of a contig — POS=1, REF=<region bases>, ALT="-", END=<last base of the region>;
  • a region that covers a whole contig — POS=1, REF=<whole contig>, ALT="-", END=<contig length>. This is not strict VCF, but it preserves deletion semantics for consensus generation.

Neither kind of block is PASS, so both are excluded from snippy.pass.vcf and only appear in the all-VCF. Both are required to rebuild the FASTA, so the recipe below selects them explicitly. The pipeline's own consensus runs on a filtered view of the all-VCF (PASS records plus the ZERODEPTH blocks), so zero-depth regions still become -; it gets its Ns from the depth BED, which step 3 reproduces from the VCF.

asm runs differ: a default asm run (no input --vcf, add_deletions_to_vcf enabled) adds ZERODEPTH deletions covering regions of the reference with no assembled sequence, but no LOWDEPTH spans, because assembly-based calling has no read-depth threshold. Only steps 1 and 2 apply to asm output; step 3 is a no-op there. If asm was given an input --vcf or deletion synthesis was disabled, its all-VCF has no ZERODEPTH blocks either.

docs.title: Rebuild the FASTA
docs.text:
With the output directory as the working directory:

REF=reference/ref.fa     # the prepared reference; the name matches your input reference
VCF=snippy.all.vcf.gz

docs.title: 1. Consensus
docs.text:
bcftools view -i '(FILTER~"PASS" || FILTER="ZERODEPTH" || FILTER="LOWDEPTHSPAN") && (strlen(ALT)<=strlen(REF) || ALT="<DEL>")' "$VCF" \
  | bgzip -c > rec.vcf.gz
bcftools index -f rec.vcf.gz
bcftools consensus -f "$REF" --mark-del - --mark-snv lc -o rec.fa rec.vcf.gz
IN_FA=rec.fa   # current FASTA; each optional step below may update it

What each part of the filter does:

  • FILTER~"PASS" — the real PASS variant calls.
  • FILTER="ZERODEPTH" — the zero-depth blocks, which are deliberately not PASS so that they stay out of snippy.pass.vcf.
  • FILTER="LOWDEPTHSPAN" — the low-depth blocks. They are intentionally not PASS either, so bcftools view -f PASS would drop both block kinds.
  • strlen(ALT)<=strlen(REF) || ALT="<DEL>" — drop insertions, whose breakpoint geometry is ambiguous for consensus, while keeping the symbolic <DEL> depth blocks (their ALT is longer than their one-base REF). This is the same pre-consensus filter the pipeline applies.
  • --mark-del - and --mark-snv lc — deleted bases become - and applied SNVs are written lowercase, matching the pipeline's pseudo-alignment. Both depth block kinds are deletions here, so both become -; step 3 turns the low-depth runs into N.

Filtered variant calls are not applied. Low-depth calls that fall inside a span are covered by the span's deletion (and then masked in step 3); a call flagged LOWDEPTH whose actual per-base position depth is not below the threshold sits outside any span and is simply excluded by FILTER="LOWDEPTHSPAN".

docs.title: 2. Mask MIXEDSITE sites (optional)
docs.text:
Flagged MIXEDSITE records are real calls, not depth regions, so they are excluded from the consensus and masked instead, exactly as the pipeline does:

bcftools query -i 'FILTER="MIXEDSITE"' -f '%CHROM\t%POS0\t%REF\n' "$VCF" \
  | awk '{print $1"\t"$2"\t"($2+length($3))}' \
  | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n | bedtools merge -i - > mixed.bed
bedtools maskfasta -fi "$IN_FA" -bed mixed.bed -fo rec.mixed.fa -fullHeader -mc n
IN_FA=rec.mixed.fa

The intervals are sorted before merging exactly as the pipeline's MaskMixedSites stage does, so the recipe mirrors the pipeline command-for-command.

docs.title: 3. Mask the low-depth regions with Ns
docs.text:
The consensus applies the low-depth blocks as deletions, but the pipeline writes N at those positions, so mask the same intervals again:

bcftools query -i 'INFO/LOWDEPTH=1' -f '%CHROM\t%POS\t%INFO/END\n' "$VCF" \
  | sort -k1,1 -k2,2n | bedtools merge -i - > lowdepth.bed
bedtools maskfasta -fi "$IN_FA" -bed lowdepth.bed -fo snippy.reconstructed.fna -fullHeader -mc N

($IN_FA is rec.mixed.fa after step 2, or rec.fa if you skipped it.)

%POS is the block's anchor base, one before the region it removes, which is exactly the 0-based start of the low-depth interval. Using %POS0 would start the mask one base early and overwrite the anchor base.

docs.title: When the result matches the pipeline
docs.text:
This recipe replays the pipeline's BcftoolsPseudoAlignment, MaskMixedSites, and ApplyDepthMaskToFasta stages on the all-VCF, so the reconstructed FASTA is byte-identical to the pipeline output whenever the reconstruction inputs agree with the pipeline's:

  • Both the LOWDEPTH spans and the pipeline's depth mask derive from the same DepthBedsFromBam min_depth_bed, so their intervals should coincide: the interval %POS–%INFO/END from a span is the same 0-based interval the BED holds. The reconstruction tests guard this invariant.
  • ZERODEPTH blocks are not PASS, so the pipeline's consensus runs on a filtered view of the all-VCF (PASS records plus those blocks); step 1 selects the same records.
  • MIXEDSITE masking uses the same intervals and the same lowercase n.

Caveats:

  • A user-supplied --mask BED (the ApplyMask step) is an external file and cannot be derived from the VCF. If you used --mask, apply that BED with bedtools maskfasta -mc X after step 3.
  • Steps 2 and 3 are both needed for the masked consensus: without step 2 MIXEDSITE bases stay unmasked, and without step 3 low-depth bases stay - instead of N. For the raw, unmasked pseudo-alignment, step 1 alone is enough.

docs.title: Index
docs.text:
Snippy-NG is organized into a small number of layers:

  • stages
  • pipelines
  • CLI subcommands

Most new features should be added by extending one of these layers rather than modifying shared execution code.

See:

  • Stages
  • Pipelines
  • CLI conventions

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
All CLI commands follow a common structure. They are defined as Click commands that use the CommandWithGlobals class and include the add_snippy_global_options decorator to add the global options. The command function then imports the appropriate pipeline builder, constructs the pipeline with the necessary arguments, and runs it with a typed runtime context. For example: 

@click.command(cls=CommandWithGlobals, context_settings={"show_default": True})
@add_snippy_global_options()
# ...pipeline-specific options...
def <name>(..., prefix, **context):
    from snippy_ng.context import Context
    from snippy_ng.pipelines.<name> import <Name>PipelineBuilder

    pipeline = <Name>PipelineBuilder(
        # pipeline-specific args only
        ...,
        prefix=prefix,
    ).build()

    run_ctx = Context(**context)
    pipeline.run(run_ctx)

docs.title: Simulation-based integration tests
docs.text: Snippy-NG has a simulation-backed integration test layer under tests/integration. These tests build synthetic datasets at test time, run the real pipeline, and check that the final VCF recovers the variants that were injected into the reference.

docs.title: Test contract
docs.text:
Each scenario defines a small set of truth variants as Python VariantRecords. The harness then:

  1. writes a truth VCF from those records
  2. applies the variants to the reference FASTA
  3. generates the requested input type
  4. runs snippy-ng
  5. compares the final VCF against the ground-truth variants

For example, this scenario:

{
    "name": "short_indel",
    "input_type": "short",
    "variants": (
        VariantRecord("Wildtype", 70, "CA", "C"),
    ),
    "untouched_regions": (("Wildtype", 200, 260),),
    "strict_region": ("Wildtype", 50, 180),
}

means:

  • apply Wildtype 70 CA C to the reference
  • simulate short reads from the mutated reference
  • run snippy-ng short on those reads
  • assert that the final VCF contains the expected deletion

This keeps each test definition small and makes the recovery requirement explicit.

docs.title: Scenario shape
docs.text:
The integration tests in test_simulated_pipelines.py are written as a simple parametrized config:

SCENARIOS = [
    {
        "name": "short_snp",
        "input_type": "short",
        "variants": (
            VariantRecord("Wildtype", 20, "A", "C"),
        ),
        "untouched_regions": (("Wildtype", 200, 260),),
        "strict_region": None,
    },
]

Fields:

  • name: scenario name used in test ids and cache paths
  • input_type: one of short, long, or asm
  • variants: truth variants to inject into the reference
  • untouched_regions: regions that should stay free of called variants
  • strict_region: optional region where only the expected truth variants are allowed

docs.title: Harness API
docs.text:
The main fixture is simulated_dataset. Each test passes:

  • an Iterable[VariantRecord]
  • an input type
  • a scenario name
  • optional untouched regions

Example:

dataset = simulated_dataset(
    (
        VariantRecord("Wildtype", 70, "CA", "C"),
    ),
    "short",
    name="short_indel",
    untouched_regions=(("Wildtype", 200, 260),),
)

The returned IntegrationDataset exposes:

  • the generated truth VCF
  • the mutated reference
  • the simulated reads or assembly
  • the output directory
  • the final called VCF
  • assertion helpers for expected and unexpected variants

docs.title: Input generation
docs.text:
The simulation code lives in simulation.py.

  • short: applies truth variants, then generates Illumina-style reads with art_illumina
  • long: applies truth variants, then generates long reads with badread
  • asm: applies truth variants and uses the mutated FASTA directly as the assembly input

The current scope is deliberately small:

  • SNPs
  • small insertions
  • small deletions

The helper rejects unsupported symbolic alleles and overlapping truth edits.

docs.title: Caching
docs.text:
Generated artifacts are not checked into git. They are created on demand and cached under .cache/integration-sim.

Cache keys include:

  • scenario name
  • input type
  • reference checksum
  • truth variant content
  • simulation parameters
  • simulator versions for art_illumina and badread

If a matching cache entry already exists, the harness reuses the generated inputs instead of regenerating them.

docs.title: Running the tests
docs.text:
Run the integration suite with:

pixi run -e integration hatch run pytest tests/integration

Run only the simulation-marked tests with:

pixi run -e integration hatch run pytest -m integration_sim tests/integration

docs.title: Pipelines
docs.text:
A pipeline is an ordered collection of stages that together perform a complete analysis. Pipelines are usually assembled by a PipelineBuilder, which decides which stages to include based on validated user input. Snippy-NG pipelines are linear: any branching happens while building the pipeline, not while executing it. For example:

class ExamplePipelineBuilder(PipelineBuilder):
    input_file: Path = Field(..., description="Input file")
    prefix: str = Field(default="example", description="Output prefix")

    def build(self) -> SnippyPipeline:
        stages = []

        first = ExampleStage(
            input_file=self.input_file,
            prefix=self.prefix,
        )
        stages.append(first)

        second = AnotherStage(
            source=first.output.result,
            prefix=self.prefix,
        )
        stages.append(second)

        return SnippyPipeline(stages=stages)

In practice, a pipeline builder usually does three things:

  • validates workflow-level inputs
  • wires stage outputs into downstream stage inputs
  • chooses which files should be kept after cleanup

Pipelines should contain workflow composition logic, not low-level implementation details. If a unit of work is independently meaningful, it should usually live in a stage and then be composed into one or more pipelines.

docs.title: Stages
docs.text:
A stage is the smallest execution unit in Snippy-NG. A stage should do one job, declare its inputs and outputs explicitly, and be reusable across pipelines. Stages inherit from BaseStage, define a typed output property, and implement create_commands() to return shell commands, shell pipelines, or Python functions to run. For example:

class ExampleStageOutput(BaseOutput):
    result: Path = Field(..., description="Output file")


class ExampleStage(BaseStage):
    input_file: Path = Field(..., description="Input file")

    @property
    def output(self) -> ExampleStageOutput:
        return ExampleStageOutput(
            result=Path(f"{self.prefix}.result.txt")
        )

    def create_commands(self, ctx) -> list[ShellCommand]:
        return [
            self.shell_cmd(
                ["cp", str(self.input_file), str(self.output.result)],
                description="Copy input to output",
            )
        ]

In practice, a stage usually contains:

  • typed input fields
  • a typed output model
  • optional dependency declarations in _dependencies
  • one or more commands in create_commands()
  • optional test_* methods for post-run validation

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The ctx argument passed to create_commands() is a runtime Context object. This contains execution settings that are not part of the stage definition itself, such as:

  • outdir
  • tmpdir
  • cpus
  • ram
  • quiet
  • skip_check

Stages should use ctx for runtime behavior such as thread counts, temporary file locations, or memory limits. User inputs that define what the stage does should remain explicit stage fields, while execution settings that affect how the stage runs should come from Context.

Stages should not contain top-level CLI parsing logic. If a task can be reused in more than one workflow, it should usually be a stage.

docs.title: Environment variable-backed stage fields
docs.text:
Stages can declare fields whose default values come from environment variables by using EnvVarField from src/snippy_ng/envvars.py. This is useful for runtime toggles that should remain part of the typed stage model rather than being hard-coded in create_commands().

For example, src/snippy_ng/stages/consequences.py defines use_local_csq like this:

from snippy_ng.envvars import EnvVarField


class BcftoolsConsequencesCaller(BaseStage):
    reference: Path = Field(..., description="Reference file")
    variants: Path = Field(..., description="Input VCF file")
    features: Path = Field(..., description="Input features file")
    use_local_csq: bool = EnvVarField(
        True,
        "LOCAL_BCFTOOLS_CSQ",
        description="Whether to use bcftools csq's --local-csq mode for consequence annotation",
    )

This field reads the prefixed environment variable:

  • SNIPPY_NG_LOCAL_BCFTOOLS_CSQ

and parse the value based on the field default type. For booleans, accepted truthy values include 1, true, yes, and on; falsy values include 0, false, no, off, and the empty string.

Use EnvVarField when:

  • the option should appear as a normal typed field on the stage
  • the value should be resolved when the stage model is instantiated
  • you want the field to participate in validation, defaults, and model introspection like other Pydantic fields

Use the typed field classes in src/snippy_ng/envvars.py (EnvVarBool, EnvVarInt, EnvVarFloat, EnvVarStr) when you need to read an environment variable outside a stage field declaration.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Snippy-NG is published on PyPI as snippy-nextgen. The command installed by the package is snippy-ng.

For most users, the installer script is the best starting point because the SNP calling pipelines depend on external bioinformatics tools as well as the Python package.

docs.title: Recommended Install
docs.text:
Install the complete Snippy-NG environment with:

curl -sSL https://cpg.org.au/snippy-ng/install.sh | bash -s -- --force

The published docs/install.sh shim downloads and runs the latest release installer from GitHub:

curl -sSL https://github.com/centre-pathogen-genomics/snippy-ng/releases/latest/download/install.sh | bash -s -- --force

After installation, check that the command is available:

snippy-ng --help

docs.title: Python-Only Install
docs.text:
Install only the Python package with:

pip install snippy-nextgen

This is enough to install the snippy-ng command and Python dependencies such as Click, Pydantic, Biopython, and NumPy. It does not install the external pipeline tools used for alignment, variant calling, masking, tree building, or read processing.

Use this option when you already manage the external tools yourself, for example with conda, micromamba, pixi, containers, or a shared HPC module system.

docs.title: GUI Install
docs.text:
The snippy-ng gui command uses Gradio, which is an optional pip extra. Install Snippy-NG with the GUI extra:

pip install 'snippy-nextgen[gui]'

Or add Gradio to an existing Snippy-NG environment:

pip install gradio

If Gradio is not installed, snippy-ng gui will print an install message and exit without affecting the rest of the command-line interface.

docs.title: External Tools
docs.text:
Snippy-NG checks stage dependencies before running a pipeline. The main external tools used by the current pipelines are:

Tool Used for samtools BAM/SAM processing, sorting, indexing, reference indexing. bcftools VCF filtering, consensus generation, consequence annotation. freebayes Short-read and optional long-read variant calling. minimap2 Short-read, long-read, and assembly alignment. bwa Optional short-read alignment. bedtools BED operations and FASTA masking. fastp Optional short-read cleaning. seqkit FASTA/FASTQ statistics and sequence utilities. rasusa Optional read downsampling. core-snp-filter Core SNP alignment filtering. iqtree Phylogenetic tree construction. longbow Clair3 model prediction for long-read runs. run_clair3.sh Clair3 long-read variant calling.

The versions used by the development environment are recorded in pyproject.toml.

docs.title: Checking An Install
docs.text:
Use --check on a pipeline command to validate dependencies without running the analysis:

snippy-ng short \
  --ref reference.gbk \
  --R1 reads_1.fastq.gz \
  --R2 reads_2.fastq.gz \
  --check

For long-read runs with the default Clair3 caller, also make sure a Clair3 model can be found or pass one explicitly:

snippy-ng long \
  --ref reference.fasta \
  --reads reads.fastq.gz \
  --model /path/to/clair3/model \
  --check

docs.title: Clair3
docs.text:
Long-read SNP calling uses Clair3 by default, but the Snippy-NG installer does not include Clair3 because it is large. Use --caller freebayes for an out-of-the-box long-read run, or install Clair3 separately.

See the Clair3 installation guide for conda, Docker, and manual environment options.

docs.title: Development Install
docs.text:
For repository development, use pixi and hatch.

git clone git@github.com:centre-pathogen-genomics/snippy-ng.git
cd snippy-ng
curl -fsSL https://pixi.sh/install.sh | bash
pixi global install hatch
pixi shell
hatch shell

Run the fast test suite with:

pixi run test

Run simulation-backed integration tests with:

pixi run -e integration test-integration

docs.title: Clair3
docs.text:
The Snippy-NG installer does not include Clair3 by default because it is large. The Clair3 environment and models are roughly 800 MB, so long-read users need to choose how they want to provide it.

Snippy-NG uses Clair3 by calling run_clair3.sh. Any installation method is fine as long as a working run_clair3.sh command is available on PATH.

docs.title: Option 1: Use FreeBayes
docs.text:
This is the simplest option and should run out of the box with the Snippy-NG installer:

snippy-ng long --ref reference.fasta --reads reads.fastq.gz --caller freebayes

This is not the preferred long-read caller, but it avoids the Clair3 dependency.

docs.title: Option 2: Install Clair3 Separately
docs.text:
Create a conda environment with Clair3 installed:

conda create -n clair3 -c conda-forge -c bioconda -y clair3

Add a wrapper called run_clair3.sh to a directory on your PATH. This example assumes ~/.local/bin is already on your PATH:

cat << 'EOF' > ~/.local/bin/run_clair3.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash

conda run -n clair3 run_clair3.sh "$@"
EOF

chmod u+x ~/.local/bin/run_clair3.sh

Check that Snippy-NG can find it:

which run_clair3.sh
run_clair3.sh --help

Then run Snippy-NG with the default long-read caller:

snippy-ng long --ref reference.fasta --reads reads.fastq.gz

docs.title: Option 3: Use Docker
docs.text:
The repository includes a Docker wrapper for Clair3:

install -m 755 docs/installation/run_clair3_docker.sh ~/.local/bin/run_clair3.sh

The wrapper runs the Clair3 container and mounts directories for common Clair3 input and output arguments. By default it uses:

hkubal/clair3:latest

Override the image if needed:

export CLAIR3_DOCKER_IMAGE=hkubal/clair3:latest

On some platforms, you may also need to set a Docker platform:

export CLAIR3_DOCKER_PLATFORM=linux/amd64

docs.title: Option 4: Install Snippy-NG With Clair3
docs.text:
You can manually create an environment that contains both Clair3 and the Snippy-NG Python package:

conda create -n clair3 -c bioconda clair3 pip
conda activate clair3
pip install snippy-nextgen

Then install any other external tools you need into the same environment. For example:

conda install -c bioconda minimap2 samtools bcftools bedtools freebayes

This works, but it is more manual than the Snippy-NG installer because you are responsible for filling in missing pipeline dependencies.

docs.title: Clair3 Models
docs.text:
Snippy-NG can use Longbow to predict a Clair3 model for read input, but the model files still need to exist somewhere accessible.

Set a model root with either:

export CLAIR3_MODELS=/path/to/clair3_models
export CLAIR3_MODEL_ROOT=/path/to/clair3_models

Or pass a model directly:

snippy-ng long \
  --ref reference.fasta \
  --reads reads.fastq.gz \
  --model /path/to/model

When using BAM or CRAM input with Clair3, pass --model explicitly:

snippy-ng long \
  --ref reference.fasta \
  --bam reads.bam \
  --model /path/to/model

docs.title: Future Conda Package
docs.text:
Once Snippy-NG is available as a conda package, the intended install path will be closer to:

conda create -n snippy-ng -c bioconda snippy-ng clair3

That package is not available yet.

docs.title: Utilities
docs.text: Snippy-NG provides utility commands that support the main SNP-calling pipelines.

docs.title: Reference utilities
docs.text:
• ref: prepare a reference genome for Snippy-NG
  • gather: discover sample files and write input for snippy-ng multi

docs.title: Alignment utilities
docs.text:
• samclip: filter clipped reads from SAM alignments using a boundary-aware terminal clipping rule
  • cnv: estimate contig or feature copy numbers from aligned BAM or CRAM depth

docs.title: Report generation
docs.text:
• tree: render an interactive phylogenetic tree report
  • sample: render an interactive per-sample variant report

See the individual command pages for usage examples and option details.

docs.title: snippy-ng utils gather
docs.text: Discover sample files and write TSV or JSON input for snippy-ng multi.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
snippy-ng utils gather --json --ref reference.gbk *.fastq.gz > samples.json

This generates a JSON or TSV file listing the samples for multi-sample analysis. See Multi-sample analysis for the config formats and options.

docs.title: snippy-ng utils ref
docs.text: Prepare a reference genome for Snippy-NG.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
snippy-ng utils ref --gbk reference.gbk -o reference

This generates the indexed reference files required by Snippy-NG pipelines.

docs.title: Alignment utilities
docs.text: Alignment utilities operate on SAM, BAM, or CRAM files produced by the mapping stages.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: Command Purpose samclip Filter clipped reads from SAM alignments. cnv Estimate contig or feature copy numbers from aligned BAM or CRAM depth.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: The samclip command is boundary-aware. A read is filtered when either terminal clip exceeds the threshold, except when the clipped end reaches the contig boundary. Fraction mode uses the total terminal clipping divided by the original query length, including hard clips.

docs.title: snippy-ng utils aln cnv
docs.text:
Estimate copy number variation from an aligned BAM or CRAM.

The command uses samtools coverage to calculate mean depth for each contig. By default, The largest contig is assumed to have one copy number. Other contigs are assigned rounded integer copy numbers from their depth relative to that baseline.

docs.title: Contig Copy Number
docs.text:
Estimate copy number for each contig:

snippy-ng utils aln cnv sample.cram > sample.cnv.tsv

Output:

contig_id   read_depth  copy_number

docs.title: Feature Copy Number
docs.text:
Supply a GFF to estimate copy number for each selected feature. By default, the first feature type in the GFF is used.

snippy-ng utils aln cnv sample.cram --gff reference.gff > sample.features.cnv.tsv

Use another GFF feature type:

snippy-ng utils aln cnv sample.cram --gff reference.gff --feature gene > sample.genes.cnv.tsv

Feature mode uses samtools depth -aa -b and reports the median per-base depth for each feature. Parsed GFF attributes are appended as additional columns. Missing attributes are reported as empty fields.

Output:

feature_id  contig_id   start   end read_depth  copy_number ID  biotype Name

docs.title: Known Single-Copy Baseline
docs.text:
Use a known single-copy interval on the largest contig as the baseline:

snippy-ng utils aln cnv sample.cram --known-single-copy-region 4518,5000 > sample.cnv.tsv

Use an explicit contig:

snippy-ng utils aln cnv sample.cram --known-single-copy-region chr1:4518-5000 > sample.cnv.tsv

The known single-copy interval can also be used with feature mode:

snippy-ng utils aln cnv sample.cram \
  --gff reference.gff \
  --known-single-copy-region 4518,5000 \
  > sample.features.cnv.tsv

Use a known single-copy feature from the GFF as the baseline:

snippy-ng utils aln cnv sample.cram \
  --gff reference.gff \
  --known-single-copy-feature gene:WILD_00001 \
  > sample.features.cnv.tsv

The baseline is the median per-base depth across the known single-copy region or feature. Feature matching uses the reported feature ID or any exact GFF attribute value, such as ID, Name, gene, or locus_tag.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Purpose ALIGNMENT Input BAM or CRAM. --gff PATH Estimate copy number per selected GFF feature instead of per contig. --feature TEXT GFF feature type to use with --gff; defaults to the first feature type in the GFF. --known-single-copy-region TEXT Baseline interval as START,END on the largest contig or CONTIG:START-END. --known-single-copy-feature TEXT Baseline feature ID or GFF attribute value from --gff. --no-header Do not print the TSV header.

docs.title: snippy-ng utils aln samclip
docs.text:
Filter clipped reads from a SAM file using a boundary-aware terminal clipping rule.

The command checks the terminal clipping at both ends of each alignment and filters the read when either end exceeds the configured threshold. If a clipped end reaches the contig boundary, that end is ignored. This means reads with large clipped segments can remain when the clipping is explained by the contig edge rather than an internal alignment artifact.

--max-clip-fraction uses the total terminal clipping divided by the original query length, including hard-clipped bases.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Filter clipped alignments with the default maximum terminal clip length:

snippy-ng utils aln samclip --index ref.fa.fai input.sam > clipped.sam

Use only the fraction-based rule:

snippy-ng utils aln samclip \
  --index ref.fa.fai \
  --max-clip-fraction 0.1 \
  input.sam > clipped.sam

Combine the absolute and fraction-based rules:

snippy-ng utils aln samclip \
  --index ref.fa.fai \
  --max 10 \
  --max-clip-fraction 0.1 \
  input.sam > clipped.sam

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Purpose SAM_FILE Input SAM file. Reads from standard input when omitted. --index PATH Reference FASTA index (.fai) for the reference used during alignment. --fix-mate / --no-fix-mate Attempt to mark mates as unmapped when one read in a pair is filtered. --max INT Maximum terminal clip length to allow on either end, after ignoring clipping at contig boundaries. --max-clip-fraction FLOAT Maximum total terminal clipping as a fraction of the original read length, including hard clips. --invert Keep only clipped reads instead of filtering them out. --debug Write debug information about clipped reads to standard error.

docs.title: Behavior notes
docs.text:
• --max is applied to each end independently.
  • A read is filtered when the left end, the right end, or both exceed the threshold.
  • Clipping at the contig boundary is ignored before the comparison.
  • --max-clip-fraction measures total terminal clipping, not just soft clips.
  • --fix-mate expects queryname-sorted SAM input.

docs.title: Report utilities
docs.text:
Snippy-NG provides HTML report generation commands under snippy-ng utils report:

  • tree: render an interactive phylogenetic tree report from a Newick tree
  • sample: render an interactive per-sample variant report from a VCF

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: Command Purpose Tree report Render an interactive phylogenetic tree report. Sample report Render an interactive sample variant report.

docs.title: Typical workflow
docs.text:
Generate a tree report after a multi-sample run:

snippy-ng utils gather --json --ref tests/data/reference.gbk tests/data/{wildtype,mutant}* > samples.json
snippy-ng multi samples.json --cpus 6 -o multi
snippy-ng tree --fast multi/core/core.095.aln -o multi/tree
snippy-ng utils report tree multi/tree/tree.snps.newick --metadata multi/snippy.qc.tsv -o multi/report

Generate a sample report from an existing VCF:

snippy-ng utils report sample short/snippy.pass.vcf -o short/report

See the dedicated pages for examples, screenshots, and command references.

docs.title: snippy-ng utils report sample
docs.text:
Create a standalone HTML report for a single sample from a VCF, with an optional embedded alignment view.

The sample report renders an interactive variant table and, when an alignment and reference are provided, an IGV.js panel showing cropped windows around each variant. It is useful for inspecting a single Snippy-NG run, sharing per-sample results, or reviewing variants before downstream interpretation.

docs.title: Example report
docs.text: Here is an example sample report generated with Snippy-NG.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
Generate a VCF-only sample report:

snippy-ng utils report sample short/snippy.pass.vcf

This writes the HTML report to:

report/sample.html

If you also provide an alignment, you must provide the matching reference.

snippy-ng utils report sample sample.vcf \
  --alignment sample.cram \
  --reference ref.fa

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
The only required input is a VCF file.

snippy-ng utils report sample sample.vcf

To embed an alignment viewer, provide both --alignment and --reference.

snippy-ng utils report sample sample.vcf \
  --alignment sample.bam \
  --reference ref.fa

The alignment can be BAM or CRAM. Snippy-NG extracts windows around each variant and embeds the cropped alignment in the final report.

docs.title: Variant selection
docs.text:
Use --variant-scope to choose whether the report includes only PASS variants or all variants in the input VCF.

snippy-ng utils report sample sample.vcf --variant-scope all

Use --window-size to control how many bases of context are shown around each variant when alignment windows are generated.

snippy-ng utils report sample sample.vcf --window-size 500

docs.title: Output options
docs.text:
By default, the command writes report/sample-report.html.

Use --outdir to choose the output directory:

snippy-ng utils report sample sample.vcf --outdir results/report

Use --prefix to choose the output filename prefix:

snippy-ng utils report sample sample.vcf --outdir results/report --prefix mutant

This writes:

results/report/mutant.html

docs.title: Report options
docs.text:
Set a custom report title:

snippy-ng utils report sample sample.vcf --title "Mutant sample report"

Override the displayed sample name:

snippy-ng utils report sample sample.vcf --sample-name mutant-01

Combine options:

snippy-ng utils report sample sample.vcf \
  --alignment sample.cram \
  --reference ref.fa \
  --variant-scope all \
  --window-size 500 \
  --title "Mutant sample report" \
  --sample-name mutant-01 \
  --outdir sample-report \
  --prefix mutant

docs.title: Command reference
docs.text:
snippy-ng utils report sample [OPTIONS] VCF
Option Default Description VCF required Input VCF file to render. --alignment, --cram, --bam none Optional BAM or CRAM alignment to embed after windowing. --reference, --ref none Reference FASTA required when --alignment is provided. --variant-scope pass Include only PASS variants or all variants. --window-size 100 Number of bases of context around each variant. --title Snippy-NG Sample Report Title shown in the HTML report. --sample-name none Optional sample name override. --outdir, -o report Output directory. --prefix, -p sample Prefix for the generated HTML file.

docs.title: snippy-ng utils report tree
docs.text:
Create a standalone HTML report from a phylogenetic tree.

The tree report renders an interactive tree and can include sample metadata, run logs, and a custom title. It is useful after running snippy-ng multi and snippy-ng tree, or any time you already have a Newick tree that you want to inspect in a browser.

docs.title: Example report
docs.text: Here is an example tree report generated with Snippy-NG.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
snippy-ng utils report tree multi/tree/tree.snps.newick \
  --metadata multi/snippy.qc.tsv

This writes the HTML report to:

report/tree.html

Open the HTML file in a web browser to view the interactive report.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
The only required input is a Newick tree.

snippy-ng utils report tree tree.newick

Metadata is optional, but recommended when you want to label, search, filter, or colour tree tips by sample fields.

snippy-ng utils report tree tree.newick --metadata metadata.csv

Supported metadata formats are:

  • CSV
  • TSV
  • JSON

Metadata rows must include one of these sample identifier columns:

  • id
  • sample_id
  • sample
  • name

The identifier values must match tip names in the Newick tree. Rows that do not match tree tips are skipped.

docs.title: Colour tips by metadata
docs.text:
Use --color-by-column to choose a metadata column for the initial tree colour scheme.

snippy-ng utils report tree tree.newick \
  --metadata metadata.tsv \
  --color-by-column lineage

The selected column must exist in the metadata file.

docs.title: Output options
docs.text:
By default, the command writes report/report.html.

Use --outdir to choose the output directory:

snippy-ng utils report tree tree.newick --outdir results/report

Use --prefix to choose the output filename prefix:

snippy-ng utils report tree tree.newick --outdir results/report --prefix outbreak

This writes:

results/report/outbreak.html

docs.title: Report options
docs.text:
Set a custom report title:

snippy-ng utils report tree tree.newick --title "Outbreak report"

Include a log file:

snippy-ng utils report tree tree.newick --logs snippy-ng.log

Midpoint-root the tree before rendering:

snippy-ng utils report tree tree.newick --mid-point-root

Ladderize the tree before rendering:

snippy-ng utils report tree tree.newick --ladderize

Options can be combined:

snippy-ng utils report tree multi/tree/tree.snps.newick \
  --metadata multi/snippy.qc.tsv \
  --color-by-column lineage \
  --logs multi/core/LOG.txt \
  --title "Snippy-NG outbreak report" \
  --mid-point-root \
  --ladderize \
  --outdir multi/report \
  --prefix report

docs.title: Command reference
docs.text:
snippy-ng utils report tree [OPTIONS] NEWICK
Option Default Description NEWICK required Newick tree file to render. --metadata none Optional metadata file in JSON, CSV, or TSV format. --color-by-column none Metadata column used to colour tree tips. --logs none Optional log file to include in the report. --title Snippy-NG Report Title shown in the HTML report. --mid-point-root off Midpoint-root the tree before rendering. --ladderize off Ladderize the tree before rendering. --outdir, -o report Output directory. --prefix, -p tree Prefix for the generated HTML file.
